passage:
Dear Yamini Bua,
I wanted to thank you for Sunday lunch.
Since I was twelve, the family has had a nickname for me that I won't write here. This year, after a term of hostel food and football, everyone suddenly said, "Wah, so slim now, finally handsome!" I know they meant it kindly. But I realised the praise and the teasing were the same thing: both about my body, both telling me that's what counts. Now I feel every eye on my plate. If I take a second roti, I wait for someone to say something.
When Chachi started on my waist again, you said, "Vishal, you've been playing so much football, are you sleeping enough?" The whole table moved on to exams.
Could you keep doing that? I think the others listen to you.
With love,
Vishal

qa.q: What did Yamini Bua ask Vishal at Sunday lunch?
qa.a: "Vishal, you've been playing so much football, are you sleeping enough?"

qa.q: What does Vishal worry about when taking a second roti?
qa.a: Vishal feels anxious and watched, expecting someone to comment on the plate.

qa.q: Which choice by Yamini Bua shifted the table, and why did it work?
qa.a: Yamini Bua turned the talk from Vishal's waist to football and sleep, focusing on health rather than looks, so the table moved on.

qa.q: Why might Chachi think those comments are harmless?
qa.a: Chachi probably means them as kindness or praise, and doesn't see that they make Vishal feel watched and valued only for looks.

grounding: It shows a young adult who, teased and then praised for their body, learns that looks are what count and feels watched at meals, until talk about health shifts the mood.

passage: People think compliments can't hurt. I'm Preeti, and I'm speaking at this wellness evening because of our college canteen. At school they called me names for being tall and bony. Then in college the same body got praise: "You should model." "Don't ever gain weight." Different words, same message: my body was the most interesting thing about me. I started to feel eyes on me at every meal. If I ate a samosa, someone said, "Careful!" If I skipped one, someone said, "Wow, discipline." So I stopped eating in the canteen at all. My roommate Pooja noticed. She didn't make a speech. One day she just said at our table, "New rule: no body talk while we eat. Tell me about your day instead." People laughed, and then they actually did it. It sounds small. It let me eat lunch again.

qa.q: What was Pooja's new rule at the table?
qa.a: No body talk while we eat.

qa.q: Why did Preeti feel watched at every meal?
qa.a: Both eating and skipping food drew comments, so Preeti felt self-conscious and judged over every food choice.

qa.q: What made Pooja's choice at the table effective?
qa.a: It was simple and friendly, swapping body talk for "Tell me about your day", so people could change the habit without feeling scolded.

qa.q: How might the people who said "You should model" see their own words?
qa.a: They probably thought they were giving compliments, not realising the praise taught Preeti that looks were Preeti's value.

grounding: It shows how teasing and praise about a body both teach that appearance is value and make meals feel watched, and how a roommate's kind table rule changes the climate.
